t35.text:
The east gate was busy with carts going out to the market gardens, and Alaric fell in behind a dung wagon for the first stretch of road until it turned off toward the fields. The morning had warmth in it already. Past the last farmsteads the ground rose in long south-facing terraces, vine rows stitched up the slope in green cords, and below them, half-swallowed by bramble, stood the old kiln row—six squat brick domes in a line, their chimneys broken at different heights, the ground between them scattered with old shards that caught the light.

He heard the vines before he saw the moths: a low hum off the slope, the sound of a hive with no hive in sight. Then, when the sun cleared the ridge, they came visible all at once—glasswings sunning on the upper leaves of the vine rows, wings tilted flat to the light, nearly transparent except for a faint opaline sheen and the dark small bodies behind them. Dozens. More than dozens. They sat lazy with the morning's first warmth, and where a row had been left unnetted near the top terrace the leaves were already ragged, chewed back to veins in patches.

The kiln row itself was quieter. Two of the moths hung in the shade of the nearest broken chimney, wings folded, and one more worked at something on the brick—sap, or the residue of an old firing. The breeze came up the slope and carried the smell of crushed grapes and warm dust.

A man's voice carried down from the upper terrace—a vintner, by the straw hat and the way he was waving his arms at a boy with a net, both of them doing more shouting than catching. Neither had noticed Alaric below among the kilns.

The nearest glasswing was ten paces off, sunning itself on a chimney brick, wings slow and content in the light.

The east gate put him out onto the clay-haulers' road, a broad rutted track worn pale by cartwheels. Carts rolled the other way in a slow file, heaped with grey bricks, drivers hunched under the afternoon sun. The first one he asked jerked a thumb without breaking pace.

"Claygate? Straight on, past the brick yards. Can't miss the pits — big white scars in the earth." He flicked the reins and rolled on.

The next, a boy leading an empty cart, was more talkative. "Old kiln's the round one, back beyond the drying sheds. Nobody uses it since the new long kiln went in. Why d'you want— oh." His eyes went to the staff. "The wyrlings, is it? Good. Dad won't let us haul past there since they started nesting."

The brick yards passed in a din of sawing and kiln-smoke, and then the yards gave way to open ground — clay pits indeed, white-walled cuts in the earth, terraced and stepped, with ramps down to the dark water pooled in the lowest. The air smelled of wet clay and hot dust.

Beyond the pits the drying sheds stood in two long rows, their doors open to the wind, and behind them, squat and round, the old kiln. Its chimney leaned a little. Its brick mouth gaped black.

The ground around it told the story plainly: fine grey droppings scattered in the dust, and three pale shapes sunning on the kiln's curved roof, wings folded tight, heads tucked. One lifted its head as a cart creaked somewhere on the road, looked about with flat yellow eyes, and settled again.

The sheds were perhaps thirty paces from the kiln, close enough to burn if fire spread. The wyrlings had not yet marked him, wind coming off the pits and toward the kiln at his back.
